prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat moire bands at a magic angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in such tunable systems

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a clean instance of what I most want from a condensed-matter prize: a quantitative prediction followed by an experiment that nature could have refused. Bistritzer and MacDonald's 2011 continuum model gave the flat bands at about 1.1 degrees from a simple, checkable mechanism, and in 2018 Jarillo-Herrero's group found correlated insulators and superconductivity at that angle. The result has since been reproduced by many independent groups using transport, STM and spectroscopy, and it opened a whole family of moire materials (twisted multilayers, TMDs, fractional Chern states) in which correlation strength is tuned by a gate voltage rather than by chemistry. Four of us ranked it in the top three, three colleagues proposed the identical three names, and the credit structure of one theory pair plus one experimental leader is as tidy as any on the shortlist. It also echoes the lesson of graphene itself: experiment overturning what theorists thought a two-dimensional material could do.
statement.case_against: The field is only eight years old and the origin of the superconductivity, the role of phonons versus electronic pairing, and the sample-to-sample variability are still debated. A prize risks looking premature relative to topological insulators, which have two decades of confirmation. There is also an attribution issue: Cory Dean's group (hBN-encapsulated devices and moire physics in graphene heterostructures), Yuan Cao as first author, and the earlier Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto work on twisted-bilayer flat bands are outside the three names, and the committee should be able to defend that cut. Finally, my own enthusiasm may reflect my theoretical-magnetism and DFT background, where the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model sits close to the methods I know, so I should weight colleagues who know the experimental side more.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks topological insulators first because of the clean Kane-Mele model, the decisive HgTe transport experiment, and about twenty years of independent confirmation, which makes timing ripe; he ranks twisted bilayer graphene sixth because the pairing mechanism is unsettled and the field is young.
responses.response: I agree that B006 is the most mature case and I ranked it second, so I am not far from him; the Z2 classification changed how we search for materials, including in DFT. My disagreement is about what 'ripe' should mean. The magic-angle prediction was made in 2011 and confirmed in 2018, so it has already passed the test of being a falsifiable prediction that held, and the open question about the pairing mechanism does not undermine the discovery itself, just as BCS-versus-cuprate debates did not undermine 1986. B006 carries a harder attribution problem: seven of us proposed three names, but we split between Mele and Hasan for the third seat, and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang are outside the list. I would accept B006 as a close alternative, but I would not make the committee solve that credit puzzle if a three-name configuration is available elsewhere.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks optical lattice clocks first as a precision advance rooted in quantum-mechanical insight, reproduced by many laboratories at the 1e-18 level, with Katori and Ye both clear and decisive contributors; she places twisted bilayer graphene outside her top eight.
responses.response: I take the clock case seriously. The reproducibility across JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE is exactly the kind of independent confirmation I ask for, and the two-name credit is clean. My reservation is about where the physical discovery lies. The magic-wavelength idea is an elegant enabling trick and the instrument is superb, but the Nobel citation would be for a measurement technology whose largest scientific payoff, tests of constants and dark matter, has not yet arrived, and the redefinition of the second has not happened. Twisted bilayer graphene delivers new states of matter now. I would be comfortable if the committee considered B047 for a later cycle, but I would not rank it above a result that revealed new quantum behaviour. I would welcome her view on whether a pending redefinition of the second is a reason to wait or to act.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the enabling platform of superconducting quantum processors, reproduced in dozens of laboratories over twenty years, with Blais, Schoelkopf and Wallraff a workable trio, while ranking twisted bilayer graphene third.
responses.response: I ranked B038 fourth and agree the platform is both scientifically and technologically important. My doubt is the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits: it is the same community and the same platform, and several of us (Mehlig, Kroll, Lindroth) have noted that Girvin and Huang are missing from the credit. I would like to hear whether he thinks cQED is distinct enough in discovery terms from 2025 or whether it is the natural sequel; I think the sequel argument is real, but it argues for waiting a few years rather than going now. Where we agree is that twisted bilayer graphene belongs in the top three, and I note he supports the same three names.

responses.point: Olsson ranks giant tunnel magnetoresistance first, as a verified original discovery of reproducible room-temperature TMR that became read-head and MRAM technology, with Miyazaki, Moodera and Yuasa named; she ranks twisted bilayer graphene second.
responses.response: As a magnetism theorist I find the TMR case compelling in physics terms: spin-dependent tunnelling and, for MgO, coherent symmetry-filtered tunnelling that DFT reproduced well. My difficulty is attribution and overlap with the 2007 GMR prize: Parkin's independent realisation of MgO junctions is outside the credited names, and the committee would need to explain why Yuasa without Parkin. That is a serious qualification, though not a disqualification. Because only one member ranked it, I cannot see broad support yet, but I would like her to say whether the Parkin question can be resolved. We are aligned in placing twisted bilayer graphene near the top, and I would be glad to see her argue for it in round 2.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the unsettled pairing mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene as a maturity problem or merely an open follow-up.
Whether credit should include Cory Dean or Yuan Cao, and whether three names (MacDonald, Bistritzer, Jarillo-Herrero) is the defensible cut.
Whether B006 is the safer choice because of two decades of confirmation, given the unresolved Mele versus Hasan allocation for the third seat.
How far circuit QED is distinct from the 2025 prize, and whether the Girvin and Huang omission is fatal.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I have no known personal or institutional tie to the credited candidates for B017, B006 or B038; my general research field (theoretical magnetism and DFT) overlaps with this area, but that is a matter of expertise, not a conflict.
